name: Aaron Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Ruth and I bought Ridgeway Farm eleven years ago, with a mortgage that'll outlive the tractor. It's 110 hectares: 90 suckler cows raising beef calves, plus wheat and oats. The cows wear GPS collars, so I move them between paddocks from my phone, with no fences to shift. Every morning I check the herd on the app, then I'm out on the quad, then I pack beef boxes we sell online. An AI assistant writes most of my customer emails and helps me plan the grazing.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Red tape. I can learn any machine in a week, but a new government form takes me a month to get right. Ruth runs a little bakery in town, and our kids are Daniel, fourteen, and Grace, eight. On Sundays I'm at church, where I'm an elder, and half the conversations after the service are about cattle prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI Plateau. I'd be a bit let down, honestly. I was hoping for a robot to do the fencing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At church I'd say the Lord gave us hands for a reason, and we'd laugh. To the other farmers I'd say keep using what works, because the collars and the apps are already worth it. I'd post a picture of the herd moving itself between paddocks, just to annoy the sceptics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it wouldn't hurt us. The beef boxes keep growing on their own merits, Ruth's bakery is busy, and the mortgage is big but steady. My worries would be the usual ones: the beef price, the weather and the 12,000 left on the tractor loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the AI further on grazing plans and the beef box marketing. I'd buy a second batch of collars for the young stock, about 3,000, in the spring. And I'd keep saving 200 a month and pay a little extra on the tractor loan each quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little disappointed. Ridgeway Farm is in good shape, and good shape without the shiny robots is still good shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not us. The older farmers at church who've had two bad years are the ones I'd keep an eye on, because a plateau doesn't fix their prices. I'd rather lend them a hand with the collars than watch them sell up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ruth say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth would say good, now you can stop talking about robots at dinner. Ruth's bakery runs on early mornings and a good oven, and she's never once asked an app about bread.

say: Keep using what works, because **the collars** and the apps are already worth it.
The Lord gave us **hands** for a reason, and a plateau means we keep using them.
think: A plateau wouldn't hurt us: **the beef boxes** grow on their own merits and Ruth's bakery is busy.
My worries stay **the beef price**, the weather and the 12,000 tractor loan.
do: Pushes AI further on **grazing plans** and beef box marketing.
Buys a **second batch of collars** for the young stock for about 3,000 in spring.
Keeps saving **200 a month** and overpays the tractor loan each quarter.
feel: **Calm** and a little **disappointed**; the farm is in good shape either way.
S0.quote: Ridgeway Farm is in good shape, and good shape without the shiny robots is still good shape.
fieldNote: Aaron is **genuinely secure** here: two busy businesses, savings and a herd run on collars and apps.
His only regret is **missing robots** for the heavy work.
Unprompted, he turned to **older farmers** at his church, who he thinks would struggle anyway.

steps.text: Push the AI further on grazing plans and beef box marketing
Buy a second batch of collars for the young stock, about 3,000
Keep saving 200 a month and overpay the tractor loan quarterly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we're talking. Forms, planning, answering customers, that's every job I hate. If the robots come slowly, I've got time to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the farmers' meeting I'd say the paperwork just got cheaper, so stop fighting it and use it. At church I'd say the ones who'll struggle are the older farmers who won't touch a phone, and we should help them rather than gossip. Online I'd just say, finally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd do well. The AI would take the forms, the grazing plans and the beef box emails, and I'd get two days a week back. The one thing I'd watch is that every beef farmer gets the same online marketing for free, so my edge on the boxes narrows. I'd still be ahead, just not as far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand every form and the beef box customer emails to the AI in the first month. I'd buy a fencing robot once a neighbour has had one a full season, about 6,000 from savings, keeping three months untouched. I'd take on an apprentice, a local lad, and charge neighbours to set up GPS collars for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly, and a bit excited. The only thing that bothers me is the men at church who'll be left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at church in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mr Brennan at my church still keeps his cattle records in a school exercise book, and AI is taking the paperwork first. He's 67 and won't let a machine near it. I'd sit with him on a Sunday afternoon and do it together, if he'd let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would an apprentice still make sense if AI does the planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More sense, not less. The planning's the bit a machine does now, but somebody still has to walk the fences and calve the heifers for years in this picture. I'd rather train a local lad than see him leave for the city.

say: The paperwork just **got cheaper**, so stop fighting it and use it.
The **older farmers** who won't touch a phone will struggle, and we should help them, not gossip.
think: I'd do well, with AI taking the forms and emails and giving me **two days a week** back.
The catch is every beef farmer gets **the same marketing**, so my edge on the boxes narrows a little.
do: Hands every form and **beef box email** to the AI in the first month.
Buys a **fencing robot** for about 6,000 from savings once a neighbour has run one a season.
Takes on **a local apprentice** and charges neighbours to set up GPS collars.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited**, troubled only by the older men at church who'll be left behind.
S1.quote: Old Mr Brennan at my church still keeps his cattle records in a school exercise book, and AI is taking the paperwork first.
fieldNote: Aaron is **the clearest winner** here: the card takes the tasks he hates and leaves his hands-on work.
He named a real risk, **his online edge** narrowing, but brushed it aside.
His concern for **an older church member** who keeps records in an exercise book was sincere.

steps.text: Hand all forms and beef box emails to the AI in month one
Buy a 6,000 fencing robot once a neighbour has proved one
Charge neighbours to set up GPS collars on their herds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the forms go first and the fencing later. I could live with that order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the cattle society I'd say it's the best news farmers have had in years: the paperwork goes in 2028 and we've got three years to get ready for the robots. I'd tell the young farmers to learn the machines now and not wait. I'd say it with a straight face, because I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased and a bit nervous at the same time. The AI doing my forms and planning the grazing is a gift, I've wanted that for years. The worry is 2031, when the big beef outfits get robots too and the price per kilo drops, and I don't want to be holding a big loan when that happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd hand every form, the grazing plan and the beef box marketing to the AI, and get two days a week back. I'd use those days to pay the 12,000 machinery loan off by 2030, not 2033, so we're clear before the price falls. I'd buy only machines that pay for themselves in a season. And I'd sell the robot know-how to neighbours, setting up their systems for a fee, while I'm the one who knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly excited. Like starting a long drive with a good map and one tyre I'm not sure about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Daniel? He'd be seventeen by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that sits in my chest. Daniel likes the cattle, but I don't know what a young stockman does when a robot can do the stock work. I'd want my son to learn the machines and the animals, so he's the one fixing them, not watching them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the older farmers at church would struggle. What happens to them here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years isn't long for a man of seventy who still uses a paper diary. I'd go round after the service with my laptop and set up the AI for their forms myself, for nothing. If I can save Mr Fenwick a month of paperwork, that's worth more than any fee.

say: It's **the best news** farmers have had in years: the paperwork goes in 2028.
Young farmers should **learn the machines** now and not wait.
think: The AI doing my forms and grazing plans is **a gift** I've wanted for years.
The worry is 2031, when beef prices drop and I don't want to be **holding a big loan**.
do: Hands every form, the grazing plan and beef box marketing **to the AI** in 2028.
Pays the **12,000 machinery loan** off by 2030 instead of 2033.
Sets up **robot systems** for neighbours for a fee.
feel: **Uneasy but mostly excited**, like a long drive with a good map and one doubtful tyre.
S2.quote: If I can save Mr Fenwick a month of paperwork, that's worth more than any fee.
fieldNote: Aaron treats the three years before robots as **a deadline** to clear his debt.
His worry is **the beef price** from 2031 and his son's future, not his own skills.
He'd spend freed time helping **older church farmers** for free.

steps.text: Hand Ridgeway's forms, grazing plan and beef box marketing to the AI
Pay off the 12,000 machinery loan by 2030 instead of 2033
Set up robot and collar systems for neighbouring farms for a fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then eight for the robots. That's my kind of timeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this rewards farmers who get on with it. Five years is enough to learn it all and be ready. I'd say that at the cattle society and to the young farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd do well. I'd have the AI running the paperwork from 2031 and robots on the farm before 2034. With two years of warning I'm caught holding debt, but with five I'm the man selling the know-how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd buy the fencing robot and feed pusher and take on an apprentice, a local lad. By year two I'd build a side business setting up robots and collars for other farms. I'd bring Daniel in during the school holidays to learn alongside the apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and energised, like spring when the grass starts moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the community lose, even if you did well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the older farmers would sell up, and the church would feel it. Machines can do the work, but they can't raise a family or run a community. That's still our job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ruth's bakery do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth's bread is hands-on, so she'd have till 2034 like me. I think people would still pay for a loaf made by someone they know. She'd use the AI for her orders, and she'd tell me to stop going on about it.

say: This **rewards farmers** who get on with it.
Five years is **enough to learn** it all and be ready.
think: I'd do well, with AI running paperwork from 2031 and **robots on the farm** before 2034.
With five years' warning I'm the man selling **the know-how**, not the one holding debt.
do: Buys the **fencing robot** and feed pusher and takes on a local apprentice in year one.
Builds a **side business** setting up robots and collars for other farms by year two.
feel: **Calm and energised**, like spring when the grass starts moving.
S3.quote: With two years of warning I'm caught holding debt, but with five I'm the man selling the know-how.
fieldNote: With eight years before robots, Aaron sees **a business opening** in teaching neighbours the machines.
His values show in his worry for **the church community** and his plan to train young people.
He thinks **Ruth's bakery** has time on its side.

steps.text: Buy the fencing robot and feed pusher and take on a local apprentice
Start a side business setting up robots and collars for other farms
Bring Daniel onto the farm in school holidays to learn the machines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten and thirteen years. Plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone to be caught out, and that the market will reward the people who prepare. I'd tell the young farmers to learn steadily. A decade is a gift if you use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd love it. I'd automate step by step so the debt never runs ahead of the money. By 2039 I'd be 56, with Daniel grown and perhaps farming with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with one robot in year one and add more only as each one proves itself. I'd take on an apprentice every two years. And I'd save 50 a month each for Daniel and Grace's apprenticeships or college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Daniel learn from the robots or from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. Either way, I'd want my son to know how to calve a cow by hand, even if a machine usually does it. There's always a night when the machine breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You asked what robots leave us to do. What's your own answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching, I think. Passing it on. If the robots do the lifting, I'd spend more time with apprentices and with the old men at church, and less time on the quad.

say: There's **no excuse** for anyone to be caught out.
**A decade** is a gift if you use it, and the market will reward people who prepare.
think: I'd love it, **automating step by step** so the debt never runs ahead of the money.
By 2039 I'd be 56, with **Daniel grown** and perhaps farming with me.
do: Starts with **one robot** in year one and adds more only as each proves itself.
Takes on **an apprentice** every two years.
Saves **50 a month** each for Daniel and Grace's apprenticeships or college.
S4.quote: I'd want my son to know how to calve a cow by hand, even if a machine usually does it.
fieldNote: With a long timeline Aaron is at ease and focused on **passing skills on**.
He answers his own question about what robots leave people: **teaching and community**.
He wants his son to keep **hands-on skills** for the night the machine breaks.

steps.text: Start with one robot in year one and add more only as each pays back
Save 50 a month each for Daniel and Grace's apprenticeships or college

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots would come in 2031 and beef prices would fall while I'm still holding loans, and three years is short to pay them down. What would help is less red tape so farmers can move quickly, and the banks giving family farms a bit of breathing room on loans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about dignity. Everyone talks about jobs and money. But a man who doesn't work loses something, and I'd want to know what the robots leave us to do.

headlineQuote: Machines can do the work, but they can't raise a family or run a community.
portrait: Aaron Okafor, 43, and his wife own **Ridgeway Farm**, with 90 suckler cows and beef boxes sold online.
He uses **AI and GPS collars** every day, alongside church, family and little patience for red tape.
With two busy businesses and savings, he's **calm** if AI stalls and calm under steady change.
Steady change takes **the paperwork** he hates, though he worries for older farmers at church.
Fast AGI makes him only **uneasy** about beef prices and loans; with more time he plans step-by-step automation.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would push beef prices down from 2031 while he's still holding loans.
whatWouldHelp: **Less red tape** so farmers can move quickly.
Banks giving family farms **breathing room** on loans.
